subtopic: Caffeine, nicotine, alcohol and other substances
subtype: Using substances to cope with stress [Actor]
passage: Every evening after the last bus left the Chandpur stand, Vidya walked behind the grain shop and lit a cigarette. It had started in March, when the school inspection was coming and her mother's knee was getting worse. The first drag loosened her shoulders for a few minutes. Then, an hour later, her chest felt tight, the worry came back louder, and she wanted another. By June she was planning her whole day around that back wall. One evening Deepika, who ran the tailoring shop next door, found her there with shaking fingers. "Is it helping?" Deepika asked. Vidya laughed, then didn't. On Monday they took the bus together to the district health centre, and Vidya asked the doctor what help there was to stop.

qa.q: Where does Vidya go to smoke every evening?
qa.a: She goes behind the grain shop after the last bus leaves the Chandpur stand.

qa.q: What did Vidya feel an hour after smoking, and what shows it?
qa.a: She felt anxious again, even more than before; her chest was tight, the worry came back louder and she wanted another.

qa.q: What turning point shows Vidya noticing the pattern, and what did she do about it?
qa.a: She saw she was planning her day around the back wall, and after Deepika's question she went to the district health centre to ask for help to stop.

qa.q: How might Deepika have felt finding Vidya with shaking fingers?
qa.a: Deepika was probably concerned, and chose a gentle question instead of a lecture.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult smoking to switch off worry who gets brief relief, then rebound anxiety and dependence, and reaches for help once she notices the pattern.

subtopic: Caffeine, nicotine, alcohol and other substances
passage:
The clinic waiting room had a fan that clicked on every turn. Gurpreet held the token slip, number 14, and read it again.
"You can still leave," Kunal said quietly beside him.
"I'm not leaving." Gurpreet stared at the floor. "Three times I said I'd only drink on Saturdays. Three times I broke it by Tuesday. Last month I missed my daughter Harleen's parent-teacher meeting because I was asleep on the sofa." He rubbed his face. "At night I think about it all the time. That's not a choice anymore."
"Coming here is the bravest thing I've seen you do," Kunal said.
The display flashed 14. Gurpreet stood, knees unsteady, and walked in to see the doctor.

qa.q: What token number did Gurpreet hold?
qa.a: Number 14.

qa.q: Why were Gurpreet's knees unsteady when the display flashed 14?
qa.a: He was nervous and ashamed, yet determined; telling a doctor felt huge, but he had already decided not to leave.

qa.q: Which signs told Gurpreet it was time to get help?
qa.a: Broken promises to cut down, constant thoughts about drinking at night, and missing his daughter's school meeting.

qa.q: How does Kunal see Gurpreet's visit to the clinic?
qa.a: Kunal sees it as strength, not failure, and calls it the bravest thing Gurpreet has done.

grounding: Shows a person recognising broken promises, strong cravings and a suffering family life, and reaching out to a doctor as an act of strength.

subtype: Toddler wound up by fast screens [Actor]
passage:
"Why is Siddharth still bouncing? It's nine-thirty," Papa sighed.
"That cartoon with the flashing colours," Parul said. "He watched it right after his bath."
Siddharth kicked his blanket off and wailed.
"Last night we read books instead, remember? He was asleep by eight-thirty."
"Okay. Tomorrow, no cartoon after dinner. Just the duck book and the song."
"Deal. Come, baby, lights low." Parul picked him up, humming, and his wail softened into hiccups.

qa.q: What did Siddharth watch right after his bath?
qa.a: That cartoon with the flashing colours.

qa.q: How was Siddharth feeling at nine-thirty, and how can you tell?
qa.a: He was wound up and cranky; he was still bouncing, kicked his blanket off and wailed.

qa.q: What plan do the grown-ups make for tomorrow?
qa.a: No cartoon after dinner, just the duck book and the song with the lights low.

qa.q: What is bedtime like for Papa on a night like this?
qa.a: It is tiring and frustrating for Papa, who sighs at seeing Siddharth still bouncing so late.

grounding: Shows a toddler wired and cranky after fast, bright videos before bed, and quiet books and a song helping him settle.

passage: The power went out in the middle of Jyoti's cartoon, just as the rabbit was about to find the key. Jyoti screamed, threw the remote and lay flat on the floor. Noor, her aunt, sat beside her in the dark. "That was sudden. You didn't get to see the end." Jyoti sobbed louder. After a while Noor lit a candle and made shadow rabbits on the wall. Jyoti peeped out from her arm. The next evening Noor said, "Five more minutes, then we feed the parrot." When the show ended, Jyoti grumbled, but she went to find the seeds.

qa.q: What did Noor make on the wall by candlelight?
qa.a: Shadow rabbits.

qa.q: Why did Jyoti scream and lie on the floor when the power went out?
qa.a: She felt upset and cheated because the show stopped suddenly, just before the rabbit found the key.

qa.q: What helped the next evening go more smoothly?
qa.a: Noor gave a five-minute warning and a pleasant next job, feeding the parrot, so the ending was not a shock.

qa.q: What is it like for Noor to sit through Jyoti's meltdown in the dark?
qa.a: It is hard and tiring, but Noor stays calm and kind, naming what happened instead of scolding.

grounding: Shows a young child melting down when a show ends abruptly, and a warning plus a pleasant next activity softening the next transition.

passage: Beta, you want the tablet in your room? Sit, and let your Hansa Dadi tell you about your papa, Deepak, when he was eleven. We gave him a video-game box for his birthday, and he kept it beside his bed. Every night I heard little beeps till past midnight. In the mornings he was a bear. He missed the school bus twice, dozed off in a maths test and shouted at me over a lost sock. Then his class teacher phoned: "Deepak seems so tired and cross lately." That night your Dadaji and Deepak sat down and agreed: games until eight, then the box lives in the drawing room. He sulked for three days. The next week he was up before me, whistling. So, where should your tablet sleep?

qa.q: Where did Deepak keep the video-game box at first?
qa.a: Beside his bed.

qa.q: What was young Deepak feeling on those mornings, and what shows it?
qa.a: He was tired and cross; he missed the bus, dozed off in a test and shouted over a lost sock.

qa.q: What turning point in the story changed Deepak's mornings?
qa.a: After the teacher's call, Dadaji and Deepak agreed on games until eight and the box living in the drawing room.

qa.q: How might Deepak's class teacher have seen him before the change?
qa.a: The teacher saw a boy who seemed tired and cross, and was concerned enough to phone home.

grounding: Illustrates a schoolchild gaming into the night who struggles to wake, focus and stay calm, and an agreed cut-off with the device outside the bedroom protecting sleep.

passage:
12:52 a.m., writing this by the phone torch, which is ironic.
Went to bed at 10:30 like a sensible person. Then: "one more video". Then Avni sent the class group a photo from the mall and everyone was replying, and I couldn't be the one who missed the joke. Then another video. My eyes are burning but my brain is wide awake, like someone left a light on inside it. Yesterday was the same, and in the morning I snapped at Mummy about the milk being cold and nearly cried in PT for no reason. Tomorrow has PT again. Okay. Plan: from tomorrow the phone charges on the kitchen shelf. If I miss something in the group, Avni will tell me at recess anyway. Swati, go to sleep.

qa.q: What time did Swati go to bed?
qa.a: Swati went to bed at 10:30.

qa.q: Why does Swati keep scrolling even with burning eyes?
qa.a: Swati is afraid of missing the joke in the class group, and the bright screen keeps the mind alert despite the tiredness.

qa.q: Is Swati's plan a good one, and what would help it stick?
qa.a: Charging the phone on the kitchen shelf removes the temptation, and remembering that Avni will share news at recess eases the fear of missing out.

qa.q: How might Mummy have felt when Swati snapped about the cold milk?
qa.a: Mummy was probably hurt or puzzled, since the snap came from tiredness, not the milk.

grounding: Shows a teenager whose one more video in bed, driven by fear of missing out and a bright screen, delays sleep and drops next-day mood.

subtype: Parents setting screen limits without a war [Response]
passage:
In their house above the cloth shop in Kasganj, phone rules used to be shouted. Parul would snatch her daughter Noor's phone at eleven, Noor would slam the door, and nobody slept well. One Sunday after lunch, Parul put a basket on the table. "I'm tired of fighting," she said. "I check shop orders in bed till midnight too, and I wake up with a headache. What if every phone sleeps in this basket from ten, mine included?"
Noor narrowed her eyes. "Yours too? Even when suppliers text?"
"Even then. They can wait till morning."
Noor asked for Saturdays till eleven, and Parul agreed. In the first week Parul slipped once, and Noor pointed at the basket, grinning. Parul put her phone in without a word.

qa.q: From what time do the phones sleep in the basket?
qa.a: From ten, and till eleven on Saturdays.

qa.q: Why did Noor narrow her eyes at the basket idea?
qa.a: Noor was suspicious and doubtful that the rule would really apply to Parul too, after months of one-sided snatching.

qa.q: What made this plan work better than snatching the phone?
qa.a: Parul explained the reason, let Noor help set the rule and followed it herself, so it felt like a family habit, not a punishment.

qa.q: How does Parul feel when Noor points at the basket?
qa.a: Parul is a bit caught out but accepts it without a word, showing the rule is fair for everyone.

grounding: Shows a parent setting a phone rule together with her teenager, explaining why and following it herself, so charging outside bedrooms becomes a family habit.

passage: Honestly, Rashmi, it started as "just checking the news". I'm Tejas, second year, and every night I'd lie down at eleven and open the feed. Flood pictures. Someone's internship at a big firm. Another flood. A school friend on a beach. By one I'd feel tight in the chest, jealous and scared at the same time, and then I'd lie awake replaying it all. Mornings were grey. In the library I kept yawning over the same page. What changed? Nothing dramatic. At ten-thirty I plug the phone in across the room and read a paperback, even a bad one. The first three nights I kept reaching for a phone that wasn't there. Now I'm asleep before midnight most nights, and the mornings feel lighter. The floods are still out there. I just meet them after breakfast.

qa.q: Where does Tejas plug in the phone now?
qa.a: Across the room, at ten-thirty.

qa.q: What was Tejas feeling by one o'clock at night?
qa.a: Tejas felt tight in the chest, jealous and scared at once, and couldn't switch off.

qa.q: Why does the paperback routine help Tejas's mood?
qa.a: It gives a calm wind-down without the tense, comparing feeds, so sleep comes sooner and mornings feel lighter.

qa.q: What might Rashmi notice about Tejas after the change?
qa.a: Rashmi would likely see Tejas less tired and yawning, and more relaxed in the mornings.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult doomscrolling at night, feeling tense and comparing and sleeping poorly, and a wind-down time with the phone away improving mood.

subtype: Working screens late into the night [Actor]
passage:
Thursday, 12:15 a.m.
Answered Gurleen's "quick question" at 10:50. Then one more email to the Delhi client. Then tidied a slide nobody asked me to tidy. Now the lights are off and my brain is still running the spreadsheet, row by row. Woke up yesterday feeling like I'd slept in a bus seat. Snapped at the chaiwala for giving me change in coins. Not fair to him. At lunch today I asked Gurleen straight out whether late replies were expected. Gurleen looked surprised: "No! I just send things when I think of them. Answer in the morning." So all this was me. New rule from tonight: laptop shut at 9:30, work chat muted, then half an hour of washing up and music before bed.
Vinita

qa.q: At what time did Vinita answer Gurleen's question?
How was Vinita feeling the morning after a late night of emails?
qa.a: Vinita felt unrested and irritable, as if after sleeping in a bus seat, and snapped at the chaiwala.

qa.q: What boundary does Vinita set, and why should it help?
qa.a: Laptop shut at 9:30, work chat muted and a screen-free half hour before bed, which gives the mind time to shift gears.

qa.q: How does Gurleen see the late-night replies?
qa.a: Gurleen never expected them and is surprised that Vinita felt pressure to answer at night.

grounding: Shows a professional answering messages late whose mind keeps buzzing at bedtime, and clear work limits with a screen-free half hour helping.

passage: After the class photo, Ramesh walked home through Jayanagar with his shoulders curled forward and his eyes on the pavement. The photographer had called out, "Tall boy at the back, stop hunching!" and some children had giggled. At home he sat folded on the sofa like a shut umbrella. His neighbour Tenzin knocked with a skipping rope. "Come, let's see who can do fifty." Ramesh dragged himself downstairs. By the tenth jump his arms were swinging; by thirty he was laughing and standing straight to count. Tenzin's mother called from the balcony, "Look how tall you both are!" Ramesh went red, but this time he didn't shrink.

qa.q: What did Tenzin bring when knocking at the door?
qa.a: A skipping rope.

qa.q: How was Ramesh feeling on the walk home, and what shows it?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and small after the giggles; his shoulders curled forward and his eyes stayed on the pavement.

qa.q: Why did the skipping help Ramesh's mood?
qa.a: Playful movement got his arms swinging and his body upright, which lifted his energy and eased the shy, slumped feeling.

qa.q: What might Tenzin have noticed about Ramesh that afternoon?
qa.a: Tenzin probably saw that Ramesh looked low and folded up, and offered a game instead of questions.

grounding: Shows a shy, sad child hunching and looking down, and playful movement and standing tall lifting his energy a little.
